## Overview

The Tigre are an ethnic group indigenous to Eritrea. They mainly inhabit the lowlands and northern highlands, especially the Gash-Barka, Anseba, and Northern Red Sea regions, with additional communities in eastern Sudan and a small population elsewhere in Sudan. They are a nomadic agro-pastoralist community and speak Tigre, an Ethio-Semitic language of the Semitic branch of the Afroasiatic family. The group is not ethnically homogeneous; its diversity is mainly organized along familial and clan lines. The Tigre include the Beni-Amer, Beit Asgede, Ad Shaikh, Mensa, Beit Juk, and Marya peoples. Tigre is also a lingua franca of the multi-ethnic lowlands of western and northern Eritrea.

The sources also state that the first Tigre converts to Islam were people living on islands in the Red Sea who adopted Islam in the 7th century, while mainland Tigre adopted Islam much later, including as late as the 19th century.

## Language & religion

Tigre is an Ethio-Semitic language of the Semitic branch of the Afroasiatic family. It is described as most closely related to Ge’ez, with a lexical similarity of 71% with Ge’ez and 64% with Tigrinya. As of 1997, it was spoken by approximately 800,000 Tigre people in Eritrea. Its dialects include Mansa’ or Mensa, Habab, Barka, Semhar, Algeden, Senhit, and Dahalik, spoken in the Dahlak Archipelago. Intelligibility among the dialects is above 91%, except for Dahalik; intelligibility between Dahalik and the other dialects is between 24% and 51%.

Since around 1889, Tigre has been written with the Ge’ez script, an abugida also called Ethiopic. Tigre speakers formerly used Arabic more widely as a lingua franca, and the language is also written in the Arabic alphabet. Ge’ez is mainly employed by the Eritrean government and Christian speakers, while Arabic script is used more commonly by Muslim speakers.

About 95% of Tigre practice Islam, while the remainder practice Christianity. Most are Sunni Muslims. Christian Tigre include members of the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the Roman Catholic Church, and the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Eritrea; they are often referred to as the Mensaï in Eritrea. Religious divisions have not been of particular concern within the Tigre.
